title: Book 8 — Urania, Chapter 22
paragraphs: Themistocles, however, picked out the best-sailing Athenian ships and went round to the springs of drinking water, cutting inscriptions on the stones there, which the Ionians read when they came to Artemisium the following day. These inscriptions ran as follows: “Ionians, you are not acting rightly in making war on the fathers of your race and trying to enslave Greece. Best of all would be for you to come over to our side; but if you cannot, then at least even now stand aside from the fighting against us, and ask the Carians to do the same. If, however, neither of these is possible for you — if you are held down by too strong a compulsion to revolt — then in the action, when we engage in battle, be deliberately slack. Remember that you are descended from us, and that our quarrel with the barbarian arose originally from you.” Themistocles wrote this, I suppose, with two things together in mind: either the inscriptions might escape the king's notice and lead the Ionians to change sides and come over to his, or, if reported and denounced to Xerxes, they might cause the Ionians to become distrusted by him, so that he would keep them out of the sea-battles.
